actual_source_row.exact_text: FIGURE 5.15 The Calvin cycle has three stages. In stage 1, the enzyme RuBisCO incorporates carbon dioxide into an organic molecule. In stage 2, the organic molecule is reduced. In stage 3, RuBP, the molecule that starts the cycle, is regenerated so that the cycle can continue. In summary, it takes six turns of the Calvin cycle to fix six carbon atoms from CO2. These six turns require energy input from 12 ATP molecules and 12 NADPH molecules in the reduction step and 6 ATP molecules in the regeneration step.

response.answer_text: In the Calvin cycle, RuBisCO catalyzes the fixation reaction by combining CO2 with RuBP, a five-carbon molecule [ev_007] [ev_001]. The resulting six-carbon compound is immediately broken down into two three-carbon compounds, 3-PGA [ev_007]. ATP and NADPH then use their stored energy to convert the three-carbon 3-PGA into another three-carbon compound, G3P, in a reduction reaction [ev_007] [ev_003]. Because the cycle makes G3P in this way, one G3P molecule can leave the cycle to contribute to carbohydrate formation, which is commonly glucose [ev_001] [ev_003]. Because the exported G3P has three carbon atoms, it takes three turns of the cycle to fix enough net carbon to export one G3P, and each turn makes two G3P molecules [ev_002]. The remaining G3P molecules stay in the cycle to regenerate RuBP, which prepares the system to fix more CO2 [ev_003] [ev_002]. ATP is also used in this regeneration of RuBP [ev_001] [ev_002].
response.short_answer: RuBisCO combines CO2 with RuBP; the resulting compound is split into two 3-PGA molecules, which ATP and NADPH reduce to G3P. One G3P leaves for carbohydrate formation, while the remaining G3P regenerates RuBP [ev_003] [ev_007] [ev_002].

response.answer_text: In the Calvin cycle, RuBisCO catalyzes the fixation reaction by combining CO2 with RuBP, a five-carbon molecule [ev_007] [ev_001]. The resulting six-carbon compound is immediately broken down into two three-carbon compounds, 3-PGA [ev_007]. ATP and NADPH then use their stored energy to convert the three-carbon 3-PGA into another three-carbon compound, G3P, in a reduction reaction [ev_007] [ev_003]. Because the cycle makes G3P in this way, one G3P molecule can leave the cycle to contribute to carbohydrate formation, which is commonly glucose [ev_001] [ev_003]. Because the exported G3P has three carbon atoms, it takes three turns of the cycle to fix enough net carbon to export one G3P, and each turn makes two G3P molecules [ev_002]. The remaining G3P molecules stay in the cycle to regenerate RuBP, which prepares the system to fix more CO2 [ev_003] [ev_002]. ATP is also used in this regeneration of RuBP [ev_001] [ev_002].
response.short_answer: RuBisCO combines CO2 with RuBP [ev_003] [ev_007]; the resulting six-carbon compound is converted into two three-carbon compounds [ev_007], and ATP and NADPH use their stored energy to convert the three-carbon 3-PGA into G3P [ev_007] [ev_003]. One G3P leaves for carbohydrate formation, while the remaining G3P regenerates RuBP [ev_003] [ev_007] [ev_002].
